summary: Defines YANG remote procedure calls and configuration nodes needed to retrieve attestation evidence about integrity measurements from a device, following the operational context of RFC 9683. It also covers logs from the roots of trust for measurement.

plainLanguage.summary: A checker asks a device, in a standard way, to show proof of what it is running, and the device answers with signed evidence.

questions: yang model for tpm remote attestation
subtitle: A standard YANG interface for asking a network device to prove, with a TPM-signed quote, what software it booted.

tldr.problem: A network operator wants to check remotely that a router or switch is running the software it should, but there was no standard management-protocol interface for collecting TPM-backed integrity evidence.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a YANG module with RPCs that carry a fresh nonce to the device, which answers with a signed TPM quote over selected PCRs, and an RPC that fetches the event logs behind those PCR values.
tldr.outcome: A verifier can request, collect and later appraise evidence from TPM 1.2 or TPM 2.0 devices using NETCONF or RESTCONF, provided the access to these RPCs is tightly controlled.

today: RFC 9684 is a Proposed Standard published in December 2024. It is not obsoleted or updated by any other RFC, and it is the YANG companion to RFC 9683.

sections.title: Why a YANG Model for Attestation
sections.content:
RFC 9684 defines the YANG Remote Procedure Calls (RPCs) and configuration nodes needed to retrieve attestation Evidence about integrity measurements from a device. It builds on the operational context of RFC 9683 and uses the terms of the RATS architecture in RFC 9334, such as Attester, composite device and Evidence.

The model requires at least one Trusted Platform Module (TPM), version 1.2 or 2.0, in the composite device, together with its software stack, or an equivalent hardware implementation. Each TPM serves as a Root of Trust for Storage, holding measurement data, and as a Root of Trust for Reporting, used to retrieve Evidence. Retrieval works by a YANG RPC that requests a quote, which exposes a rolling hash of the security measurements held inside the TPM.
sections.plainLanguage: A device has a tiny locked safe (the TPM) where it keeps a running fingerprint of what it started up. This RFC says how a checker can politely ask the device to show that fingerprint.

sections.title: Challenge-Response and Freshness
sections.content:
The module lets a composite device act as an Attester in the challenge-response interaction model. The YANG client, acting as the Verifier, sends a challenge, and the device answers with Evidence.

The client MUST supply a fresh nonce with an appropriate amount of entropy. This gives proof of freshness for the Evidence and prevents replay attacks. The nonce must come from an entropy source external to the Attester. A TPM nonce is typically 160 or 256 bits (20 or 32 bytes): a shorter value is padded with leading zeros inside the quote, and a longer one is trimmed to the most significant bits.

How each TPM relates to the specific measured component inside the composite device is out of scope.
sections.plainLanguage: To stop someone replaying an old answer, the checker hands over a brand-new secret number each time. The device has to put that number into its signed answer, so an old answer cannot be reused.

sections.title: Features, Identities and Data Nodes
sections.content:
The ietf-tpm-remote-attestation module has four optional features. mtpm means several TPMs on the device can support attestation, for example one per line card. bios covers BIOS and UEFI event logs, ima covers Linux Integrity Measurement Architecture logs, and netequip_boot covers network equipment boot logs. Identities for the log types are bios, ima and netequip_boot.

The data nodes sit under the container rats-support-structures. Its tpms container describes each TPM: firmware version, quotable PCRs, associated certificates and operational status. Because a certificate is tied to a TPM attestation key, knowing the certificate identifies a specific TPM. The attester-supported-algos container lists which TCG signing and hash algorithms the platform offers, so an operator can limit what the RPCs may use. The compute-nodes container, present with mtpm, maps each TPM to the compute node (such as a line card) it belongs to.

A pcr index is a uint8 in the range 0 to 31. Without an explicit choice, the hash defaults to TPM_ALG_SHA256 for TPM 2.0 and TPM_ALG_SHA1 for TPM 1.2.
sections.plainLanguage: The model is like a form with boxes: which safes the device has, which keys go with them, and which math tricks the device knows. The checker can only pick things that appear on the form.

sections.title: The Quote RPCs
sections.content:
Two RPCs fetch signed PCR values through the TPM Quote operation. tpm12-challenge-response-attestation works with TPM 1.2 devices, and tpm20-challenge-response-attestation works with TPM 2.0 devices. Where the mtpm feature is active and no certificate-name is given, all matching TPMs respond.

For TPM 2.0 the input carries a nonce-value, a tpm20-pcr-selection list (a hash algorithm and the PCR indexes to read from that bank) and optional certificate names. The output has, per TPM, the certificate-name, the TPMS_QUOTE_INFO blob, a quote-signature, an up-time and optionally unsigned PCR values. The TPM 1.2 version takes a list of pcr-index values and returns a TPM_QUOTE2 blob.

The RFC's example challenge asks for PCRs 0 to 7 from a SHA-256 bank. The example reply carries the raw quote, which includes a composite digest of the requested PCRs, the nonce and TPM 2.0 clock information, plus a signature made by the TPM key.
sections.plainLanguage: The checker says: here is my secret number, please read me lines 0 to 7 of your fingerprint list and sign it. The device sends back the signed reading.

sections.title: Retrieving Event Logs
sections.content:
A PCR value alone is only a hash. To see which events were folded into it, the Verifier uses the log-retrieval RPC to acquire the Evidence that was extended into specific PCRs.

The input names a log-type (BIOS, IMA or netequip boot) and a log-selector that picks where to start: after a given last entry, a given index number, or a timestamp. A log-entry-quantity limits how many entries come back. The output lists, per node, the log result for the chosen type.

BIOS entries have an event number, event type, PCR index, a list of digests per hash algorithm, and event data. IMA and netequip boot entries carry a template name, a filename hint, the file data hash and its algorithm, a template hash, the PCR index and optionally a signature.
sections.plainLanguage: The signed fingerprint says something changed but not what. The log is the diary of every step, so the checker can read exactly what was started and in what order.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The module is meant to be reached through NETCONF over SSH or RESTCONF over HTTPS, with access limited by the NACM access control model. Several writable nodes need care: a compromised certificate being selected or a wrong certificate type could mislead a Verifier, and the algorithm lists in attester-supported-algos could be filled with algorithms the physical TPM does not support. A vendor should restrict configuring unsupported algorithms.

The RPCs can leak information. Logs hold digests of the boot and operating system software, which a passive attacker could use to find software versions and target known vulnerabilities. Quote responses expose internal operational state that could also be correlated to running software. The RFC therefore says the RPCs should be protected by NACM with a default setting of deny-all, so only authorized Verifiers can extract attestation data.

Requesting a large volume of logs could also use significant resources and create a denial of service. Receivers of a quote response must check that the signing certificate really belongs to an active attestation key on the targeted TPM.
sections.plainLanguage: The device's fingerprint list tells a lot about what it runs, so only trusted checkers should be allowed to ask for it, and nobody should be able to flood the device with questions.

sections.title: IANA Registrations and the Algorithm Module
sections.content:
The RFC defines two YANG modules. The second, ietf-tcg-algs, mirrors the TCG algorithm registry as YANG identities such as asymmetric, symmetric, hash and signing algorithms, plus features tpm12 and tpm20 for algorithm support in each TPM version.

IANA registers both namespace URIs in the XML registry and both modules in the YANG parameters registry, with the prefixes tpm and taa. Security guidance for the algorithm module is to take care when selecting algorithms, since some TCG algorithms are considered legacy.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC also adds a dictionary of the math methods TPMs know, and the official registry office records the names of both new pieces so nobody else uses them.

sections.title: IMA and Network Equipment Boot Logs
sections.content:
Appendix A explains Linux IMA, which extends measured boot to applications and files by measuring them before execution. IMA keeps an ordered list of measurements in kernel space, the Stored Measurement Log, and is typically anchored in TPM PCRs. Templates define which fields a log record has, and policies define which files are measured. If no policy is defined, no measurements are taken.

Appendix B describes network equipment boot logs, which combine boot and operating system component measurements into one log in the IMA format. A Verifier can replay the log to compute the expected PCR value and compare it with the PCR Evidence, so it can pinpoint mismatching entries that may indicate tampered components.
sections.plainLanguage: The appendices explain the diary the device keeps while starting up, so a checker can replay it and see exactly which step looks wrong.
